title: Have mercy on me (Psalm 50 [51])
hook: David's psalm after his great sin, prayed every Friday morning

segments.voice: Yesterday, be still, two words spoken in the middle of an earthquake. Your line was be still and see. Did you drop your hands for five seconds? Today, the most famous of the sorrowful psalms. Day one hundred seventy-one.

A prophet named Nathan walks into the king's palace with a story. There were two men in a town, he says. One was rich, with flocks and herds. The other was poor, and had one little ewe lamb that he raised with his children, that ate from his plate and slept in his arms. A traveler came to visit the rich man, and the rich man didn't want to use one of his own sheep. So he took the poor man's lamb and served it for dinner. King David is furious. That man deserves to die, he says. And Nathan looks at him and says four words.
screen: `A PROPHET WITH A STORY.` → `THE POOR MAN'S ONE LAMB.` → `DAVID IS FURIOUS.`

segments.voice: "Thou art the man." David had taken another man's wife, Bathsheba, and when she was pregnant, he arranged for her husband Uriah to die in battle. He'd hidden it for months. Now it's out. And David, a king who could have had the prophet killed, says, "I have sinned against the Lord." The heading of Psalm 50 in the Douay, 51 in most Bibles, ties it to this moment. Its Latin first word gives it its name: Miserere, have mercy. "Have mercy on me, O God, according to thy great mercy." What follows is what many readers call the fullest picture of repentance in the Bible. It doesn't make excuses. It asks to be washed. "Thou shalt sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed: thou shalt wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow." Hyssop was a small plant used to sprinkle water in purification rites, and that verse is why a priest sprinkling holy water over a congregation has traditionally been called the Asperges, from its Latin. Then the center of the psalm: "Create a clean heart in me, O God: and renew a right spirit within my bowels." Create is the word from Genesis, the thing only God does. David isn't asking for a cleaned-up heart. He's asking for a new one. And near the end: God doesn't want a burnt offering; "a contrite and humbled heart, O God, thou wilt not despise." The Church prays this psalm every Friday morning in the Liturgy of the Hours, the day Jesus died. And it's the psalm behind a famous piece of music, Allegri's Miserere, said to have been so guarded by the Sistine Chapel that copies were forbidden, until a fourteen-year-old Mozart, the story goes, heard it and wrote it down from memory.
screen: `THOU ART THE MAN.` · `WHITER THAN SNOW.` · `CREATE A CLEAN HEART.` · `EVERY FRIDAY MORNING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray the first verse. Settle, and breathe. Let the psalm's first line be the only thing in your mind: have mercy on me, O God, according to thy great mercy. Say it slowly, once on each out-breath. Don't go looking for your worst sin; just let the line find whatever needs it. If you pray, stay with those words to God for the whole two minutes. If you don't, let the word mercy be the thing you breathe, for yourself and for someone you find it hard to forgive. The bell holds the time.
Miserere. Latin for have mercy, the first word and the name of David's psalm after his great sin. Today's word.
Your line: a clean heart. Today, when you catch yourself making an excuse, stop halfway, and just say what happened. Day one hundred seventy-one.

howItsDone: Catholics who pray the Liturgy of the Hours say the Miserere every Friday at Morning Prayer; it is one of the seven penitential psalms, and its verse about hyssop gave its name to the Asperges, the sprinkling with holy water.

original.note: Latin: have mercy on me, O God, the psalm's first words in the Vulgate.

trapdoor: what you thought: a sad, old prayer for forgiveness.
what it means: David's psalm after his great sin: no excuses, wash me, create a new heart in me.
what a scholar hears: create translates bara, the Genesis verb used only of God; the Asperges is named from verse 9, and Allegri's setting is said to have been guarded by the Sistine Chapel.

notes: Douay wording of 2 Kings 12:7, 12:13 and Psalm 50:3, 9, 12, 19: confirm against a Challoner edition.
Psalm 51 at Friday Morning Prayer in every week of the four-week psalter. Confirm.
Asperges me: the antiphon for the sprinkling rite is Psalm 50:9 (Vulgate). Confirm.
Mozart and Allegri's Miserere (1770, aged 14): famous story, from Leopold Mozart's letters; hedged 'the story goes'. The ban on copies is traditional; confirm.
Hebrew bara (create) used only with God as subject: a standard observation. Confirm.

Review pass: softened "the most complete picture of repentance in the Bible" to "what many readers call the fullest picture" (a judgment, not a settled fact), and hedged the Sistine Chapel ban on copies as "said to have been" in the teach and trapdoor.
David's sin is described as taking another man's wife; some modern readers stress it as an abuse of royal power over Bathsheba. A Keeper may want to review that framing.
